options: based on private information about the firm's future earnings and dividends
driven by reasons unrelated to information about value, such as a health expense or a tax bill
carried out only by professional market makers who quote bid and ask prices
that follows chart patterns in the stock's past prices to forecast moves
explanation: Noise traders buy or sell for personal or liquidity reasons (health, taxes, bills due), not because they have analysed value. Their trades can push prices away from fair value for a while (L04 s51).

stem: The disposition effect is the tendency of investors to:
options: buy stocks only after they have fallen
sell all stocks at the end of the tax year
sell winning stocks too early and hold losing stocks too long
hold diversified portfolios regardless of price
explanation: The disposition effect is a behavioural bias: realising gains feels good and realising losses feels bad, so investors sell winners and keep losers regardless of the stocks' future prospects.

stem: Early in April a retiree sells a block of shares she still likes in order to pay her income tax bill. This is an example of:
options: Noise trading
The disposition effect
Overconfidence
Momentum investing
explanation: She is selling for a personal cash need (taxes due), not because she thinks the stock is overpriced. That is noise trading. The disposition effect would require selling because of gain/loss on the position.

stem: An investor sells a stock that has doubled to 'lock in the gain' but keeps a stock that has lost 40%, saying 'I will sell when it gets back to what I paid.' This behaviour is:
options: Noise trading
The disposition effect
Sentiment
Weak-form efficiency
explanation: Selling the winner and holding the loser, anchored on the purchase price, is the textbook disposition effect.

stem: A day trader believes she can out-guess the market and trades several hundred times a month, even though her results are no better than the index. Which behavioural factor does this illustrate?
options: The disposition effect
Noise trading for tax reasons
Semi-strong efficiency
Overconfidence
explanation: Overconfidence leads investors to overestimate their ability and trade too much. The excess trading costs money and adds noise to prices.

stem: After a long bull market, a wave of optimism lifts the prices of many tech stocks well beyond what their earnings forecasts justify. This is best described as:
options: The disposition effect
Liquidity noise from tax selling
Sentiment among investors
Strong-form efficiency
explanation: Sentiment is a shared mood (optimism or pessimism) that moves prices independently of fundamentals. It is one of the behavioural reasons prices may deviate from fair value.

stem: How do noise trading and behavioural biases differ as reasons why prices may deviate from fair value?
options: Noise comes from personal or liquidity needs; behavioural biases are systematic psychological errors
Noise trading is illegal, whereas behavioural biases are legal, and only the first can move prices
Noise trading affects only bonds, whereas behavioural biases affect only stocks and no other securities
They are the same thing described with different names, so the distinction has no content
explanation: The slide groups them as two sources of mispricing: Noise (selling for personal reasons such as health, selling when bills like tax are due) and Behaviour (disposition effect, overconfidence, sentiment).

stem: Why can noise trading move a stock's price away from its fair value?
options: Noise traders always possess valuable private information about the firm
Noise trading changes the firm's future dividends and therefore its true value
The pressure has nothing to do with value, so it can push the price until others step in
Noise trading forces the firm to reissue its shares at lower prices
explanation: Fair value comes from expected cash flows. A forced seller shifts supply without changing those cash flows, which temporarily lowers the price below value until buyers who notice the discount arrive.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons for price deviations listed in the course?
options: Selling for personal reasons such as health
Firms paying dividends at fixed dates every year
Selling when bills such as tax are due
Overconfidence and sentiment among investors
explanation: The slide lists noise (personal and tax-driven selling) and behaviour (disposition effect, overconfidence, sentiment). A regular dividend calendar is not a source of mispricing.

stem: Many investors sell losing stocks in late December to realise tax losses, pushing some prices below value with no news about the firms. What could a disciplined investor do?
options: Buy at the depressed price, expecting the discount to vanish when the selling ends
Sell the same stocks short to ride the decline caused by tax-loss selling
Avoid the stocks, because in an efficient market prices are always right
Wait for the next dividend payment before deciding whether to buy
explanation: If price pressure comes from non-informational selling, the discount should reverse once it ends. Capturing it requires patience and capital, which is why such deviations can persist.

stem: A stock falls 12% on heavy volume in the last week of December with no company news, then recovers most of the loss in January. Which explanation is most consistent with the course?
options: The market learned bad private information in December and good news in January
The market is strong-form efficient, so price changes without news are impossible
Tax-related noise selling pushed the price below fair value, and it recovered when the pressure ended
The dividend was cut in December and restored in January, moving the price
explanation: A sharp fall with no news that reverses is the signature of non-informational selling (here, tax selling). An information-driven move would not reverse on its own.

stem: True or false: selling a stock to pay for a medical bill, rather than because of a view about its value, is an example of noise trading.
options: True
False
explanation: True. The seller is motivated by a personal cash need (health), which is unrelated to information about the firm; the course lists 'selling for personal reasons such as health' as noise.

stem: Investors who hold on to losing stocks while selling their winners are showing the _____ effect.
options: momentum
disposition
efficiency
dividend
explanation: The disposition effect is the habit of selling winners and holding losers.
